modelInfo.title: Model Information
modelInfo.content:
📦 BASIC MODEL PARAMETERS

• Weight (grams): Total plastic weight needed for the model including supports. Measured in grams.
  → Affects: Material cost directly
  → How to measure: Use slicer software (Cura, PrusaSlicer) for accurate calculation

• Print Time (hours): Total time the printer spends printing the model.
  → Affects: Electricity and equipment depreciation
  → Important: Take time from slicer + 10-15% safety margin

• Batch Mode: Printing multiple identical models at once.
  → Benefits: Time savings on prep, efficient bed usage
  → How it works: Weight can be per model (with multiplication) or for entire batch
  → Example: 5 keychains at 10g = 50g total

• Weight Per Model (toggle):
  → ON: Entered weight will be multiplied by batch count automatically
  → OFF: Entered weight already accounts for entire batch

materials.title: Material Costs
materials.content:
💰 MATERIAL COST CALCULATION

Formula: (model weight ÷ spool weight) × spool price

• Spool Price: What you paid for the filament spool
  → Standard weights: 1000g (1kg), 500g, 250g
  → Tip: Include shipping cost in spool price calculation

• Spool Economics: Understanding true material cost
  → Example: 1kg spool for $20 = $0.02 per gram
  → 50g model = 50 × 0.02 = $1.00 for material

• Measurement Accuracy:
  → Use slicer weight, not CAD model weight
  → Don't forget supports (add 10-30% to weight)
  → Brim and other helper elements also have weight

• Different Materials:
  → PLA: Cheapest, standard choice
  → PETG: Slightly more expensive, stronger
  → ABS, Nylon: Specialty materials, higher cost

time.title: Time & Labor
time.content:
⏱️ THREE TIME TYPES

1. Preparation Time (before print):
   • Bed preparation (cleaning, applying glue)
   • Loading and configuring file
   • Calibration if needed
   → Typical: 10-15 minutes (0.17-0.25 hrs)

2. Print Time (during):
   • Actual printer running time
   • Affects electricity and depreciation
   → Important: Take from slicer, don't round down

3. Post-processing Time (after print):
   • Removing model from bed
   • Removing supports
   • Sanding, painting (if needed)
   → Typical: 15-30 minutes (0.25-0.5 hrs) depending on complexity

💼 LABOR PAYMENT

• Hourly Rate: What your time is worth
  → Consider: Your skills, experience, market
  → Minimum: Cover operational costs
  → Optimal: Competitive rate for your region

• How it's added to price:
  → Preparation + Post-processing = Your active time
  → Print time is NOT paid as active work
  → This is the basis for calculating your labor cost

⚡ ELECTRICITY CALCULATION

Formula: print time × consumption (kW) × tariff

• Printer Consumption:
  → Ender 3: ~0.15-0.20 kW average
  → Prusa i3: ~0.10-0.15 kW
  → Large printers: 0.30-0.50 kW
  → Tip: Measure with watt meter for accuracy

• Filament Dryer:
  → When to use: Hygroscopic materials (Nylon, PETG, TPU)
  → Consumption: 50-150 W (0.05-0.15 kW)
  → Modes:
     - During print: Time = print time
     - Separately: Specify drying time manually

electricity.title: Electricity
electricity.content:
⚡ ELECTRICITY CALCULATION

Formula: time × consumption (kW) × tariff ($/kWh)

• Printer Consumption:
  → Measure real consumption with watt meter
  → Don't confuse peak and average consumption
  → Average consumption: during active printing

• Typical Consumption Values:
  → Ender 3: 0.15-0.20 kW (150-200 W)
  → Prusa i3 MK3: 0.10-0.15 kW
  → Artillery, Creality CR: 0.20-0.25 kW
  → CoreXY large: 0.30-0.50 kW

• Filament Dryer:
  → When needed: PLA when humid, PETG, Nylon, TPU always
  → Consumption: 50-150 W depending on model
  → Sunlu S1: ~70 W
  → Esun eBOX: ~100 W

• Dryer Operation Modes:
  → "During print": Dryer runs entire print time
     - Time = print time
     - Added to printer consumption
  → "Separately": Pre-print or post-print drying
     - Specify drying time manually
     - Calculated separately

• Tariff:
  → Check current tariff with your provider
  → Consider day/night rate difference (if applicable)
  → USA 2026: ~$0.12-0.15/kWh average

depreciation.title: Depreciation & Wear
depreciation.content:
📉 DEPRECIATION CONCEPT

Depreciation is spreading equipment cost over its useful life.
Why it matters: You need to recover your equipment investment.

🖨️ PRINTER DEPRECIATION

Formula: (printer cost ÷ lifespan in hours) × print time

• Example:
  → Printer: $400
  → Lifespan: 5000 hours
  → Depreciation: $400 ÷ 5000 = $0.08 per hour
  → 3-hour print: $0.08 × 3 = $0.24

• Realistic Lifespan:
  → Budget printers (Ender 3): 3000-5000 hrs
  → Mid-range (Prusa, Artillery): 5000-8000 hrs
  → Premium (Prusa XL, Bambu X1): 8000-12000 hrs

🔧 NOZZLE WEAR

Formula: (nozzle cost ÷ lifespan) × print time

• Brass Nozzle:
  → Cost: $2-5
  → Lifespan: 500-1000 hrs (depends on filament abrasiveness)
  → With PLA: ~1000 hrs, with fillers: ~200-300 hrs

• Hardened Nozzle:
  → Cost: $10-20
  → Lifespan: 2000-5000 hrs
  → For abrasive materials (carbon, metal, wood)

🛏️ BED WEAR

Formula: (bed cost ÷ lifespan) × print time

• PEI Surface:
  → Cost: $15-30
  → Lifespan: 3000-5000 hrs or 500-1000 prints

• Glass Bed:
  → Cost: $10-20
  → Lifespan: 2000-4000 hrs (depends on mechanical damage)

• Magnetic Surface:
  → Cost: $20-40
  → Lifespan: 1500-3000 hrs (sensitive to high temps)

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

• True Cost: Without depreciation you don't cover all expenses
• Replacement Planning: Know when you'll save for new equipment
• Competitiveness: Fair pricing that covers all costs
• Scaling: Understand ROI when buying new printer

business.title: Business Parameters
business.content:
📊 MARKUP

What it is: Your profit layer on top of cost, expressed as percentage.

Formula: final price = cost × (1 + markup/100)

• How it works:
  → 100% = Break even (final price = cost × 2)
  → 200% = Triple costs (final price = cost × 3)
  → 300% = Quadruple costs (final price = cost × 4)

• Examples:
  → Cost: $10
  → Markup 100%: $10 × 2.0 = $20 (profit $10)
  → Markup 200%: $10 × 3.0 = $30 (profit $20)
  → Markup 50%: $10 × 1.5 = $15 (profit $5)

• Factors for Setting Markup:
  → Market competition
  → Model complexity
  → Service uniqueness
  → Turnaround time
  → Your expertise level

• Recommendations:
  → Standard models: 100-150%
  → Complex models: 150-250%
  → Rush orders: 200-300%
  → Custom design: 250-400%

⚠️ FAILURE RATE

What it is: Statistical buffer for prints that fail.

Formula: cost with failures = base cost × (1 + failure/100)

• How it works:
  → 10% adds 10% to all costs
  → Covers: Material, time, electricity for reprints
  → Applied BEFORE markup

• Example:
  → Base cost: $10
  → Failure 10%: $10 × 1.1 = $11
  → Then markup 200%: $11 × 3.0 = $33

• Recommended Values:
  → Simple PLA: 5-10%
  → Complex models: 10-15%
  → Experimental materials: 15-25%
  → TPU, Nylon: 20-30%

• Risk Factors:
  → Geometry complexity (many supports)
  → Model height (adhesion risk)
  → New material (insufficient experience)
  → Long prints (more risk points)

🔄 HOW THEY INTERACT

1. Base cost (material + electricity + depreciation + labor)
2. + Failure rate (statistical buffer)
3. = Cost with risks
4. × Markup = Final price
5. - Cost = Your profit

Complete calculation example:
→ Base cost: $12
→ Failure 10%: $12 × 1.1 = $13.20 (cost)
→ Markup 150%: $13.20 × 2.5 = $33 (final price)
→ Profit: $33 - $13.20 = $19.80

additional.title: Additional Costs
additional.content:
➕ CUSTOM EXPENSES

What it is: Project-specific costs not covered by base categories.

• Typical Examples:
  → Packaging (boxes, bubble wrap)
  → Shipping (post, courier)
  → Special materials (magnets, keychain rings)
  → Painting (paints, varnish)
  → Post-processing (putty, primer)

🎚️ "INCLUDE IN BASE COST" TOGGLE

Important parameter affecting calculation:

• ON (Include in Fee = ON):
  → Expense becomes part of base cost
  → Affected by failure rate
  → Markup applied to it
  → Use for: Production-related costs

  Example: Magnets for each keychain ($2)
  → With failure 10%: $2 × 1.1 = $2.20
  → With markup 200%: $2.20 × 3.0 = $6.60 in final price
  → Your profit accounts for this expense

• OFF (Include in Fee = OFF):
  → Expense added to final price directly
  → No failure or markup
  → Simply "pass-through" cost
  → Use for: Costs you don't control

  Example: Shipping via courier ($8)
  → Simply added: final price + $8
  → No profit on shipping
  → Client pays exact cost

📦 "PER ITEM" TOGGLE

For batch mode (more than 1 model):

• ON (Per Item = ON):
  → Expense multiplied by model count
  → Each model needs this expense separately
  
  Example: Keychain ring $0.50, batch of 10
  → Total expense: $0.50 × 10 = $5
  → Use for: Fasteners, magnets, individual packaging

• OFF (Per Item = OFF):
  → Expense applies to entire batch
  → One expense for all models together
  
  Example: Shipping box $3, batch of 10
  → Total expense: $3 (regardless of count)
  → Use for: Set packaging, batch shipping

💡 USAGE STRATEGIES

1. Production Costs (Include in Fee ON):
   → Paints, varnish → with markup
   → Special fasteners → with markup
   → Magnets, screws → with markup

2. Pass-through Costs (Include in Fee OFF):
   → Shipping costs → without markup
   → Bank fees → without markup
   → Client expenses → without markup

3. Combined Approach:
   → Base box ($3) → OFF, per batch
   → Magnet each ($0.50) → ON, per item
   → Shipping ($8) → OFF, per batch

olx.title: OLX Commission
olx.content:
🛒 OLX MARKETPLACE

What it is: Popular marketplace in Ukraine for selling goods.

OLX Commission Structure:
→ 2% of item price
→ + $0.80 fixed fee per transaction

📊 TWO CALCULATION MODES

Your mode choice depends on HOW you sell models:

1️⃣ "PER ITEM" MODE (Per Item = ON)

Use when: Selling each model as separate listing

Formula: (model price × 1.02 + $0.80) × model count

Example: Keychain $5, made 5 pcs, selling separately
→ Commission for 1: $5 × 1.02 + $0.80 = $5.90
→ Commission for 5: $5.90 × 5 = $29.50
→ You receive: $29.50 from clients
→ Net profit: $29.50 - ($5×5) = $4.50

When to use:
✓ Selling individually to different clients
✓ 5 separate listings for 5 keychains
✓ Each model - separate OLX transaction

2️⃣ "BATCH" MODE (Per Item = OFF)

Use when: Selling all models as one set

Formula: (total price × 1.02) + $0.80

Example: Set of 5 keychains, total price $25
→ OLX commission: $25 × 1.02 + $0.80 = $26.30
→ You receive: $26.30 from one client
→ One transaction, one commission

When to use:
✓ Selling set to one client
✓ One listing "Set of 5 keychains"
✓ Single OLX transaction

🎯 COMPARISON EXAMPLE

Scenario: 5 models at $5 each (total $25)

📌 Individual Sales (Per Item ON):
→ Client price per item: $5.90
→ 5 transactions at $5.90 = $29.50 total
→ OLX commission: ($5×1.02+$0.80)×5 = $4.50
→ You keep: $29.50 - $4.50 = $25 (your price)

📦 Batch Sale (Per Item OFF):
→ Client price for set: $26.30
→ 1 transaction at $26.30
→ OLX commission: $25×1.02+$0.80 = $26.30 - $25 = $1.30
→ You keep: $26.30 - $1.30 = $25 (your price)

Difference:
→ Individual: Clients pay more ($29.50 vs $26.30)
→ Batch: More economical for client, faster sale

💡 STRATEGY CHOICE

✅ Sell INDIVIDUALLY when:
→ High-demand items (keychains, figurines)
→ Different clients buy 1 pc each
→ Have time for multiple listings
→ Can get higher total revenue

✅ Sell as BATCH when:
→ Sets that go together
→ Want to quickly sell entire batch
→ Client wants multiple at once
→ Save on OLX commission

⚠️ IMPORTANT

• Calculator shows price FOR CLIENT (including commission)
• You receive your stated price minus OLX commission
• Commission is always deducted from you as seller
• Mode choice doesn't affect your profit, only client price
